analysis.one_liner: Bars former Members of Congress from certain lobbying jobs for five years instead of one.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, never received a committee vote or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Current federal law bars former members of Congress from lobbying their former colleagues for one year after leaving office. This bill would have stretched that 'cooling-off' period to five years, making it harder for ex-lawmakers to immediately cash in on their connections. It was introduced in May 2003 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would get a government in which former lawmakers cannot immediately convert their congressional connections into lucrative lobbying work, reducing the 'revolving door' between Congress and K Street.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends section 207(e)(1)(A) of title 18, U.S. Code, changing the post-employment lobbying restriction from one year to five years for former Members of Congress.
The CRS summary confirms it amends the federal criminal code to lengthen from one to five years the period during which former Members may not engage in certain lobbying activities.

analysis.who_pays: Former members of Congress and the lobbying firms that hire them, who would lose the ability to sell recent insider access to clients for four additional years.

drawbacks.text: A five-year ban could push former lawmakers out of public service entirely or deter qualified people from running for Congress, and it restricts the livelihood of people leaving office, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.
Longer bans may simply drive former members into 'shadow lobbying' roles that fall outside the legal definition of lobbying, reducing the rule's practical effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit of reducing the revolving door is real, though a five-year ban also imposes a genuine restriction on ex-lawmakers' careers and may be partly avoided through work that technically falls outside 'lobbying.' The bill is simple and well-targeted, but it was never debated or refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews (D-NJ) introduced the bill on May 20, 2003; no other member cosponsored it.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction.
On June 25, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former members of Congress and lobbying firms are better off, since the one-year cooling-off period remained in place and the stricter five-year ban was never enacted.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend the post-congressional lobbying ban to five years.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred, letting it die in committee.

against.name: House Subcommittee on the Constitution
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from June 2003 onward without taking it up.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and never reached a vote, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have reduced the pool of recently departed lawmakers available to lobby for five years after leaving office. Its death preserves their access to former members with fresh connections.
Ex-lawmakers keep the one-year restriction rather than a five-year bar, preserving their ability to sell congressional access quickly. The bill never became law, so this advantage continues.
